scaling_analysis_stage_d.quantum_complexity: O(√N) queries (provably optimal — BBBV lower bound)
scaling_analysis_stage_d.crossover_estimate: No practical crossover identified: with a naive O(N)-gate oracle there is none, and with a structured oracle the quadratic query saving is not expected to pay for error-correction overhead on early fault-tolerant hardware (Babbush et al., arXiv:2011.04149)
scaling_analysis_stage_d.honest_assessment: Grover speedup is provably optimal but quadratic. The oracle compilation cost is the critical variable: a naive oracle implementing the function as a circuit costs O(N) gates, completely eliminating the speedup. Only structured oracles with O(poly(n)) gate cost preserve the advantage.

advantage_claim_contract.fairness_rationale: Brute-force is optimal for unstructured key search (no exploitable structure in properly designed ciphers)
advantage_claim_contract.quantum_resource_scaling: Grover achieves O(sqrt(N)) — provably optimal quadratic speedup (BBBV)

residual_risks: Quadratic speedup only: it halves the effective key length and does not break modern cryptography

scaling_analysis_stage_d.crossover_estimate: No practical crossover identified: AES-128 needs about 2^64 Grover iterations run in series, about 2^86 T gates on 2,953 logical qubits (Grassl et al., arXiv:1512.04965), and quadratic speedups are not expected to pay for error-correction overhead on early fault-tolerant hardware (Babbush et al., arXiv:2011.04149)
scaling_analysis_stage_d.honest_assessment: Grover's quadratic speedup is provably optimal but only halves the effective key length, and only if its iterations run in series. NIST expects Grover to give little or no advantage against AES and considers AES-128 secure for decades to come (NIST PQC FAQ). The practical threat to modern cryptography is from Shor (factoring) not Grover (search).
